At the height of the trade war between Trump and China, new tariffs were being announced almost every week, and companies like Logitech responded by sharply raising the prices of their products in the United States.

Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that these tariffs were illegal and must be refunded to manufacturers. However, no company has yet been seen passing those refunds on to consumers, and a class-action lawsuit is now underway to try to correct the situation…

The Trump Tariff Saga

Last year, Trump seized on the U.S. trade deficit with China, making a loud show of announcing sweeping tariffs on Chinese-made products in a bid to force companies like Apple to shift production back to the United States.

Such talk was, of course, never realistic. The U.S. lacks the infrastructure, expertise and cheap labour needed to support mass production of consumer electronics.

Trump has always insisted that the tariffs would be borne by China, but the reality is that it was American brands importing goods from China who paid the duties, and the extra cost was ultimately passed on to consumers through price hikes. At its peak, the tariff rate reached a staggering 145%.

Take Logitech as an example — the company raised prices on roughly half of its products by as much as 25%.

Consumers Should Get a Refund

The U.S. Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and ordered the repayment of amounts already paid by U.S. businesses. The refund process is now underway.

The issue is that the costs were ultimately borne by consumers through higher prices, yet none of the affected companies have so far signalled any intention to refund their customers.

Law firm CPM has filed a class-action lawsuit against Logitech over the matter, seeking refunds for consumers who paid the inflated prices while the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac's Take

The principle at stake here is indisputable. Businesses paid the tariffs, passed the extra cost on to consumers, and now the government is refunding the money to the businesses. Morally speaking, they ought to return the excess amounts they collected to consumers who bought the products during that period.

In practice, however, it is likely to be extremely difficult. Logitech would have to identify every single transaction completed through a vast number of third-party retailers, track the actual prices paid by consumers, and work out what portion of that was attributable to the tariffs.

Even if this lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it could set a very interesting precedent — though it must be pointed out that in class actions, it is usually the lawyers who benefit, while the compensation eventually received by consumers tends to be very small.
